summary: This RFC proposes a protocol that returns the user identification for a TCP connection. It is the second draft, superseding RFC 912, with a more formal syntax for requests and responses and a specified identification type. It was replaced by RFC 1413.

plainLanguage.summary: This proposal lets a host ask who owns a particular TCP connection. It specifies a port-pair query and a response with a system name and user identifier, while warning that the answer depends on trusting the remote host.

questions: what is the authentication server protocol
subtitle: A proposal to identify the user associated with a TCP connection.

tldr.problem: An application may need to identify the user who owns an existing TCP connection on another host.
tldr.mechanism: A server listens on TCP port 113 and accepts a query containing the local and foreign port numbers of a fully specified connection, then returns a user identifier or an error.
tldr.outcome: The proposal describes possible uses and warns that applications must decide how much to trust each server. RFC 1413 later replaced it.

today: RFC 931 was replaced by RFC 1413. It records a proposed authentication-server protocol and its cautions about trusting returned identifiers.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The Authentication Server Protocol provides a way to identify the user of a particular TCP connection. Given the connection's pair of port numbers, the server returns a character string identifying the connection owner on its system. The RFC suggests uses such as FTP user identification and verification for network services.

Only fully specified connections may be queried. A user on one host can ask the other host only about connections between those two hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol asks a host to identify the user associated with a TCP connection. The query is limited to a connection between the host making the request and the host answering it.

sections.title: Query and Response Format
sections.content:
The server listens for TCP connections on port 113. After a connection is established, the client sends one line containing the target system's local port and the source system's foreign port, separated by a comma. The server replies with the same pair and either USERID or ERROR, followed by information about the result.

A USERID response names an operating system and gives an identifier in that system's format. ERROR responses may report INVALID-PORT, NO-USER, or UNKNOWN-ERROR. The server closes the query connection after sending the identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends two port numbers to the server on TCP port 113. The reply either gives the operating system and user identifier or explains why the user could not be identified.

sections.title: Trust and Suggested Uses
sections.content:
The RFC warns that authentication servers on different hosts may not be equally trustworthy. Applications using a returned identifier must decide how much confidence to place in it; the RFC notes that restricting use to a locally controlled subnet may be appropriate in some cases.

Suggested applications include automatic identification during FTP, checking users for privileged operations, and avoiding a second login for some terminal users. The memo describes these as proposed or experimental uses.
sections.plainLanguage: A returned name is only as trustworthy as the server that supplies it. Each application must decide whether the answer is reliable enough for its purpose.

sections.title: Status of the Proposal
sections.content: RFC 931 describes itself as a proposed protocol and asks the ARPA-Internet community for discussion and improvements. The unit metadata records RFC 1413 as its replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC presents a protocol proposal for discussion. RFC 1413 later replaced it.
